summary: Gives information about preparing RFCs and some policies on publishing them. It is guidance for authors, not a protocol. It was replaced by RFC 2223.

eli5.summary: A how-to guide for people writing these memos, telling them how to format and submit.

subtitle: A 1993 style guide telling authors how to format, label and submit an RFC.

tldr.problem: Many people write memos for the RFC series, and the RFC Editor needs them to be consistent and readable on a wide variety of printing and display equipment.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1543 sets editorial policy, strict ASCII and PostScript format rules, the layout of headers and footers, required sections, and the meaning of the terms UPDATES and OBSOLETES.
tldr.outcome: It obsoleted RFC 825 and RFC 1111, and has itself been obsoleted by RFC 2223.

sections.title: What the RFC Series Is and How Files Are Shared
sections.content:
This memo gives information about preparing RFCs and some policies on publishing them. The series covers a broad range of interests: the core topics are the Internet and the TCP/IP protocol suite, but any topic related to computer communication may be acceptable at the discretion of the RFC Editor. Anyone may submit a memo. A large source is the IETF, whose working groups evolve Internet Drafts until they are reviewed by the IESG and sent to the RFC Editor.

RFCs are distributed online as public access files. Because the files are printed or displayed on a wide variety of equipment, the primary RFC is always an ASCII text file. A secondary version may be provided in PostScript to include diagrams and drawings, but PostScript was found to be harder to search, excerpt in e-mail, and produce consistently.
sections.eli5: Memos are saved as plain text so any computer or printer can show them. Fancy versions are allowed, but the plain one is the real one.

sections.title: Editorial Policy and Review
sections.content:
Documents proposed as RFCs are reviewed by the RFC Editor and possibly other reviewers. The review may suggest improvements, redirect the author to coordinate with an IETF Working Group, conclude the document is not appropriate, or add a statement about ideas that are relevant but inappropriate or unsafe. The RFC Editor may make minor style and format changes, and sometimes changes to the text, but more often returns the memo to the author.

Standards track documents must be approved by the IESG before reaching the RFC Editor. The IESG communication usually names the exact Internet Draft, and the RFC Editor assumes only that file is to be processed. Small corrections should be sent separately, or as a diff, not as a new version.

Since the ASCII version is primary, a PostScript version must match it, and the RFC Editor decides if it is the same. Authors may query the RFC Editor about status, but not more than once a week.
sections.eli5: An editor reads each memo and may send it back with suggestions. If a fancy copy exists, it has to say exactly the same thing as the plain one.

sections.title: ASCII and PostScript Format Rules
sections.content:
Authors must submit an editable online document, ideally matching the style of recent RFCs. For ASCII, each page is limited to 58 lines followed by a form feed on a line by itself, and each line to 72 characters. There is to be no overstriking or underlining, no extra spaces to force a straight right margin, no hyphenation at the right margin and no footnotes. Text is single spaced with one blank line between paragraphs. Cross references by section number are easier to keep right than by page number.

For PostScript, the standard page is 8 1/2 by 11 inches with 1 inch margins. Main text is no smaller than 10 points with 12 point line spacing, and notes no smaller than 8 points with 9.6 point spacing. Helvetica, Times Roman and Courier (with bold and italic versions) are the acceptable fonts, and a list of commands such as initgraphics and erasepage must not be used.
sections.eli5: The rules are like a school worksheet: only so many lines on a page, no squished tiny writing, and only a few kinds of lettering allowed.

sections.title: Headings, Status and Required Sections
sections.content:
The first page heading has the traditional Network Working Group line, Request for Comments: nnnn, the author's initial and last name, the organization, the month and year, an Updates or Obsoletes line if any, and the category: Standards Track, Informational, or Experimental. The title is centered below. From page 2, a running header has the RFC number, a title and the date, and every page has a footer with the author's last name and [Page N].

Each RFC must have a Status of this Memo section with one of three standard statements, an Introduction that explains motivation and applicability, and a References section in the RFC style (including STD numbers where assigned). It must also have a Security Considerations section near the end and, at the very end, an Author's Address section with name, postal address, telephone and e-mail.
sections.eli5: Every memo wears the same name tag at the top and has the same parts in the same order, so readers always know where to look.

sections.title: UPDATES and OBSOLETES
sections.content:
When an RFC adds to or replaces an earlier one, two terms are used. UPDATES marks a supplement that cannot stand alone and must be added to the earlier document. OBSOLETES marks a document that replaces an earlier one and can be used alone. The terms SUPERSEDES and REPLACES are no longer used.

In lists of RFCs or the RFC-Index, but not in the RFCs themselves, the pointers OBSOLETED-BY and UPDATED-BY may be used with early documents to point to later ones. The RFC also tells readers to see STD 1 for protocol standards, gives the RFC Editor's contact address, and describes two mailing lists used for announcements.
sections.eli5: If a new memo is only an add-on, it says UPDATES. If it fully takes the old memo's place, it says OBSOLETES.

sections.title: The nroff Appendix and Its Sample Memo
sections.content:
Most RFCs are processed with the Unix nroff program using the ms macro package, and authors who prepared their memo this way are asked to say so. The appendix gives the command pipeline, a small sed script and a C program called pg that fix up form feeds so pages break correctly.

It then appends a sample memo prepared in RFC style. That sample is the text of RFC 1149, dated 1 April 1990, a joke document about carrying IP datagrams on birds. The Security Considerations section of this RFC itself says it raises no security issues, with a pointer to Section 6.
sections.eli5: At the back is a tool recipe for lining up pages and an example memo, which happens to be a funny one about delivering messages with birds.
